# Summary of the analysis approach 

The SMARVUS dataset$^{1}$ was initially cleaned by removing columns that were not relevant to the research question. Demographic and educational information, such as gender, language and previous level of mathematics study, was retained alongside questionnaire responses for further exploration.

The respondents were then filtered. Only students whose grades were provided directly by their universities were included to ensure consistency in comparisons, as self-reported grades could describe modules sat years before the questionnaire. Observations where grades were recorded as zero were also  excluded, as these could be null submissions. 

The 70 respondents who did not fully complete all four anxiety questionnaires (STARS, R-MARS-S, STARS-M and R-MARS) were also excluded to ensure consistency when calculating and comparing anxiety scores. England and Northern Ireland were grouped together to simplify geographical comparison. Furthermore, respondents who failed any of the attention checks, or who did not confirm that they had answered the survey truthfully, were excluded. This resulted in the exclusion of another 342 respondents. 

This left a final sample of 1,385 respondents across 18 universities in 10 countries, with questionnaires completed in seven languages. The geographical distribution of the final sample is presented in Table 1.

The relationship between statistics anxiety and academic attainment was investigated using a meta-analysis, treating each university as a separate study. This approach was chosen to account for differences in grading systems and allow for investigation of variation in effect sizes across universities.

# Details of the analysis

## Accounting for differences in grading systems

A key challenge when comparing attainment in statistics modules across universities is the diversity of grading systems. Some universities use percentage-based grades, whilst others use alternative numerical scales or letter-based grading systems. Furthermore, the same percentage attainment may correspond to different levels of achievement across universities.

By treating each university as a separate study, the original numerical grading scales can be retained, avoiding the potential loss of information associated with converting all grades to a common scale.

## Calculating anxiety scores

The SMARVUS dataset contains four measures of statistics and mathematics anxiety (STARS, R-MARS-S, STARS-M, & R-MARS). STARS and R-MARS-S measure statistics anxiety, whilst STARS-M and R-MARS measure mathematics anxiety. Each questionnaire consists of either 20 or 23 items, with responses recorded on a five-point scale. The overall anxiety scores were calculated by summing the individual responses for each questionnaire, with higher scores indicating greater levels of anxiety. STARS was selected as the primary measure of statistics anxiety for this analysis, as it directly measures anxiety in statistics-related situations.


## Preliminary analysis: University of Sussex

The University of Sussex was initially selected as a case study to demonstrate the approach before extending it to the wider dataset. Following the data cleaning and filtering process outlined above, 320 responses from the University of Sussex were retained. Grades at this university were reported as percentages, allowing for a direct investigation of the relationship between statistics anxiety and academic attainment. 

Descriptive statistics were calculated for both STARS scores and academic attainment. The mean STARS score was 70.09, with a standard deviation of 18.20 and a median of 70. Histograms were produced to further investigate the shape, spread and symmetry of both distributions.



```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 7, fig.align="center", fig.cap="Distributions of statistics anxiety and academic attainment at the University of Sussex."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

hist(smarvus_sussex$stars_score,
     col = "steelblue",
     main = "Statistics Anxiety",
     xlab = "STARS Score",
     ylab = "Frequency")

hist(smarvus_sussex$grade,
     col = "indianred1",
     main = "Academic Attainment",
     xlab = "Grade (%)",
     ylab = "Frequency")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Figure 1 shows the distributions of statistics anxiety and academic attainment at the University of Sussex. The distribution of STARS scores is approximately symmetrical and bell-shaped, centred around a mean of 70.09. In contrast, the distribution of academic attainment is negatively skewed, with most respondents achieving grades between 60% and 80%. A small number of considerably lower grades contribute to the longer left tail. These observations are worth considering when investigating the correlation between statistics anxiety and academic attainment, as extreme values may influence Pearson's correlation coefficient.

Having explored the distributions of statistics anxiety and academic attainment individually, a scatterplot was produced to investigate the relationship between the two variables. It was hypothesised that higher levels of statistics anxiety would be associated with lower academic attainment.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 6, fig.cap="Scatterplot of attainment vs statistical anxiety."}
# Seeing relationship between anxiety and attainment
ggplot(smarvus_sussex,
       aes(x = stars_score, y = grade)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, col = 'steelblue') +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", col = 'indianred1') +
  labs(
    x = "STARS Score",
    y = "Grade (%)",
    title = "Statistics Anxiety and Attainment at Sussex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```
Figure 2 shows a slight negative correlation between STARS Score and attainment, suggesting that respondents with higher levels of statistical anxiety tend to perform worse. Pearson's correlation coefficient, a measure of the strength and direction of the linear relationship, was calculated to be -0.20, with a 95% confidence interval of [-0.30, -0.09]. This suggests a statistical significance. 

The correlation coefficient was then converted into Cohen's d to obtain a standardised effect size to allow for comparison of effect sizes across universities and their subsequent pooling through a meta-analysis. The Cohen's d measure calculated to be -0.41, indicates a small to moderate effect size$^{2}$, suggesting that higher levels of statistics anxiety are associated with lower academic attainment at the University of Sussex. 

## Extending analysis across universities

Having demonstrated the analytical approach using the University of Sussex, the same methodology was applied to the remaining universities to investigate whether the observed relationship between statistics anxiety and academic attainment was consistent across different universities and countries. 

Pearson's correlation coefficient was calculated independently for each university and subsequently converted into Cohen's d to obtain comparable effect sizes.

## Meta-analysis

To investigate the overall relationship between statistics anxiety and academic attainment, a meta-analysis was conducted, treating each university as a separate study and pooling the individual effect size estimates.

### Choice of meta-analysis model

There are two main approaches to pooling effect sizes: fixed effect (assumes  that one true effect size exists in the population) and random effect (assumes that the true effect varies).$^3$ Given the differences in educational settings, demographics, teaching methods and assessment systems across universities, a random effect model was chosen.
